children: KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia--AirAsia hasn't sought a government bailout or had aircraft grounded or repossessed over nonpayment, co-founder and adviser Tony Fernandes said.

The comments came at a briefing Friday after a news report said the Malaysia's government had asked Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air whether they could absorb AirAsia's domestic market share as authorities monitor its financial health. The report sent AirAsia shares down 21% Thursday.

Fernandes denied receiving government assistance or knowing of any discussions with other airlines about AirAsia's domestic market share. He said his sources told him the government had held no such talks.

Malaysia's Finance Ministry, which the report said was involved in the talks, wasn't immediately available for comment. State-linked airport operator Malaysia Airports Holdings said it was unable to comment on the matter when contacted.
Fernandes said that creditors have remained supportive, and the airline's planned $1 billion fundraising is largely intended to refinance existing debt at lower interest rates and on better terms.
He said the current situation amid geopolitical tensions is far less severe than the Covid-19 pandemic, when the airline faced a much deeper crisis.
"Covid was far, far worse than what we are dealing with now," he said.

The second quarter was the most challenging because tickets were priced based on lower oil prices before fuel costs rose sharply because of the Iran war, he said. Fernandes expects the impact to reverse in the third and fourth quarters as fuel costs and cash flows catch up.

AirAsia's third-quarter load factor is about 80%, he said, with strong demand expected to continue into the fourth quarter. The airline cut about 60 routes because of the Middle East crisis but plans to restore 25 in the second half as operations stabilize.
